items.bodyEn: At Maisaka, the thirtieth post town, the Tōkaidō ran into water. Lake Hamana was freshwater until an earthquake and tsunami in 1498 broke through its sandbar; the breach was named Imagire, 'the new cut', and the lake turned brackish. Travelers crossed by boat, about four kilometers to Arai and its barrier. Hiroshige painted sails and fishing stakes, Fuji behind.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō No. 31 Maisaka: Imagire shinkei; 明応地震 (1498) records

items.bodyEn: 守 puts 寸, a hand, under 宀, a roof: someone keeping watch over a house or office. The Shuowen Jiezi defines it as the official who keeps a government hall. Hence mamoru (守る), to protect, and sekimori (関守), the keeper of a barrier. 留守 (rusu) once meant staying behind to guard the house; today it means nobody is home.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (説文解字), entry 守; Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (日本国語大辞典), entry 留守

items.bodyEn: This station's ppoi means 'has a strong flavor of', and the flavor is often one you did not order: kodomoppoi is childish, yasuppoi looks cheap, wasureppoi is forgetful. For the admiring sense use rashii: kodomorashii is charmingly childlike, harurashii is just as spring should be. Same noun, opposite warmth.

Wataru seken ni oni wa nai: the world you pass through holds no demons. People are kinder than you fear, and strangers will help a traveler. Wataru, to cross, is the verb for fording rivers and for getting through life, so the saying fits a station where the road itself turned into a boat.
items.ja: {渡|わた}る{世間|せけん}に{鬼|おに}はない
items.kana: わたるせけんにおにはない
